L.A. festival highlights need for more Afro Latine spaces

Culture
by Isaac Ceja
All photos and video by Isaac Ceja
08.13.2026 | share +
BlueskyThreadsLinkedInShare
Listen to audio version of this article
0:00 / 4:08
Instaread

When Chuck Maldonado spoke with AfroLA, he wore a one-of-a-kind shirt: a frog donning an NYC hat and wheat-colored Timberlands in front of a Puerto Rican flag, with “Black Rican Vegan” emblazoned below. For 30 years, he’s worked as a creative director for mega events like the 1996 Olympics in Atlanta, a dancer and choreographer for artists like Jennifer Lopez, popular TV shows, and movies including “Stomp the Yard.” He’s lived in Los Angeles for 25 years, and said he wishes there were more area events celebrating the rich history and culture that the local Afro Latine community has to offer.

Earlier this month, the fourth annual Afro-Latino Culture Fest attracted hundreds of people to dance, drink, eat, enjoy a variety of performances, and celebrate their Afro Latinidad. 

Across LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes near Union Station attendees proudly displayed their countries’ flag. Some had shirts, others wore hats and a couple of people even draped a flag over themselves as they danced.

“There are a lot of Dominicans, Puerto Ricans, Cubans, Panamanians, Colombians. and There’s so many Afro Latinos that live in this community,” Maldonado said. “I wish that we had more gatherings like this, especially because we have such great weather here in L.A.”

The festival’s performances were Afro Latin dance and music styles Maldonado loves: Bachata, salsa, merengue and bomba. All of these are rooted in the fusion of traditional African rhythms and movements by Indigenous peoples in Latin America and the Caribbean resulting from migration and slavery.  

The Afro-Latino Culture Fest is the signature event of the Afro-Latino Education and Arts Collective (ALEAC), a community-driven nonprofit dedicated to advancing education, cultural preservation, and social equity for Afro Latines. 

ALEAC founder Sharon Cruz hopes attendees walk away with more connections than they did before they walked in.

“Culture is one of the most powerful bridges we have,” Cruz said. “It reminds us that although we come from many nations, we share the same heartbeat.” 

Much like Maldonado, some attendees AfroLA spoke with said they enjoyed the fest but wished to see more events, more representation, and more support for the Afro Latine community in the region. 

In 2019 there were 2.2 million “Afro-Latinxs” in the United States, according to a UCLA Latino Policy and Politics Institute study. That’s a 121% increase since 2000, growth twice the rate of non-Black Latines in the same period.

Festival vendor Lymaira Agosto, an Afro Boricua artist, proudly described why she displays pre-colonial art like paintings featuring Taina —the name for the Indigenous Arawak people—and a person wearing a Vejigante mask. 

“I have gotten a lot of support today especially from other Boricuas,” Agosto said. “They’ve been saying they have not seen a lot of Boricua art, especially representation to the culture and especially pre-colonization as well.”

Though she’s only lived in L.A. for a year and a half, Agosto said she’s surprised how difficult it’s been to find authentic Puerto Rican restaurants or Afro Latine culture,  arts, and events. She said that she hopes to be a part of the change bringing more representation of the culture with her art.

“Representation matters…I really think that’s important,” Agosto said. “Everybody needs to feel welcome in some way.”

Cousins Courtney Williams and Nairobi Hilaire Seabrooks came to celebrate Williams’s birthday. Both said that they feel the term “Latino” does not always include Afro Latines. 

“Latino you don’t really see it in terms of popular media being and including Black people, so it means a lot that like not only do we get to recognize it, we get to recognize it together…we are Afro Latina,” said Hilaire Seabrooks whose family is from French Guadeloupe in the West Indies 

Williams said she loves seeing the spectrum of skin tones reflecting diverse nationalities and identities gathering in the same place.“There’s literally everybody here, you know. And I just love that,” she said. “There’s so much love here. It’s amazing.”
